# PHP - Debugging Curl

When you are handed a pre-existing PHP class that relies on `curl_setopt()` and `curl_exec()`, inspecting the outgoing payload isn't just a matter of printing variables; it requires understanding how cURL constructs its internal buffers before execution. The specific need here is to see what POST fields are actually being serialized into the HTTP request body before `curl_exec()` sends the bytes over the network.

Since you cannot easily modify the existing class, you must either intercept the data at the point of construction or enable verbose output from cURL itself. The most direct approach within the PHP language is to inspect the value stored in the handle's context before execution occurs. However, `CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS` does not always contain a simple associative array ready for printing; it often gets transformed into a raw string or an `@resource` depending on how the library was configured.

If the underlying class stores the fields in a variable like `$options['CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS']`, you can access that directly. However, if the value has already been converted to a string (e.g., via `http_build_query()`), printing it will show the URL-encoded string rather than the original field names and values. To debug this without altering the source code of the third-party class, you can rely on cURL's built-in verbosity flags.

The standard method for observing raw traffic is enabling verbose output. By setting `CURLOPT_VERBOSE` to `true`, cURL will echo every line it sends and receives to the standard output or error stream. This includes headers, cookies, and the request body. To make this useful in a script, you typically redirect the output of `curl_exec()` to `stderr` or capture it if the handle is passed through a specific callback function.

Another powerful technique involves enabling `CURLOPT_STDERR`. When combined with verbose mode, this allows cURL to write its debug log to a specific stream. If your application runs in an environment where you can control file descriptors, you might redirect `STDERR` to a log file or pipe it directly to the terminal. This reveals exactly what the library sends, including any internal headers or multipart boundaries if those are involved.

For deeper inspection without modifying the existing class, you can wrap the call in a try-catch block and inspect the handle properties immediately before execution. Specifically, checking `$handle->info['http_code']` is post-execution, so that won't help for debugging the request body itself. Instead, look at the options array passed to `curl_setopt`. If the library uses an associative array for options, you can temporarily modify the value assigned to `CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS` right before the class calls `curl_exec()`.

If modifying the call site is impossible and you only have access to the final output, enabling `CURLOPT_HEADER` along with `CURLOPT_VERBOSE` in your own wrapper around the class is a viable strategy. You create a new handle, clone or duplicate the existing one if possible, set `CURLOPT_VERBOSE = 1`, and then execute. Note that simply setting these options on the handle does not automatically print them; you must ensure the output stream is directed to your logger or stdout.

There is also the option of using cURL's built-in debugging feature which allows writing debug data to a file. This is often achieved by passing the output of `curl_exec()` through error handling, though standard PHP cURL does not have a direct "write verbose log to file" option like libcurl has in C. Instead, you rely on the stream redirection capability.

One critical pitfall to avoid is assuming that `CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS` always reflects the original array. If the library sets the option with a stringified version of the data, inspecting the variable will show the encoded payload, not the logical fields. In such cases, enabling verbose output via `CURLOPT_VERBOSE` remains the only reliable way to see the exact bytes sent.

If you are working in a Laravel environment or similar framework where you might eventually refactor this logic, consider creating a trait that wraps any cURL handle with automatic verbosity logging. This trait would set `CURLOPT_VERBOSE` and redirect `STDERR` to a dedicated debug channel before execution, ensuring future maintenance is easier.

For production environments, always remember to disable verbose mode once debugging is complete. Leaving `CURLOPT_VERBOSE = 1` in production can leak sensitive information like headers or partial payloads in logs, violating security best practices. Ensure that your logging configuration filters out these verbose cURL outputs unless specifically intended for troubleshooting a specific incident.
